abstract: Boryl groups are among the most versatile functionalities in modern chemistry, yet their electronic effects remain poorly quantified. Hammett substituent parameters provide a powerful framework for describing substituent effects, but are available for only a limited number of boryl groups. Herein, we combine experimental measurements and computational approaches to establish a comprehensive set of Hammett constants for the most commonly used boryl substituents. Experimental determination was achieved through acidity measurements of meta- and para-substituted benzoic acids and complemented by computational methods for systems inaccessible to direct measurement. The resulting parameters reveal an unexpectedly broad range of electronic behaviors, spanning strongly electron-donating tetracoordinate borates to highly electron-withdrawing dihaloboranes and boranes. Analysis of inductive and mesomeric contributions, supported by Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) calculations, identifies the key structural factors governing these trends, including boron coordination state, heteroatom-to-boron donation, and π-acceptor ability. These results establish a quantitative framework for understanding, comparing, and predicting boryl substituent effects, providing a foundation for the rational design of boron-containing reagents and functional molecules.
hook: Measured Hammett constants show boryl groups range from strong electron donors to strong acceptors.
summary: The authors measured how boryl groups shift the acidity of substituted benzoic acids and filled gaps with calculations. Four-coordinate borates push electrons strongly, while dihaloboranes and boranes pull them. Some values come from computation, not measurement, because those systems could not be measured directly.
title: A Quantitative Map of Boryl Substituent Effects Through Hammett Parameters and Electronic Analysis.
